all_of: a request value reaches eval() or an equivalent evaluator, with only a character filter in front of it
the filter is a DENYLIST of characters rather than an allowlist of an expression grammar
the denylist leaves the sigils intact: at minimum ~ and parentheses, and ideally $ { } [ ] . ^ as well
the runtime is PHP 7.x, where an undefined constant evaluates to its own name as a string
any_of: a length cap that rules out long XOR-chain payloads and forces a compact one
no string literal is possible at all because both quote characters are filtered

signals: dont bite the hand that feeds you human
report to the nearest galactic federation agency

chain.action: map the filter one character at a time over the whole printable set, sending each candidate inside a harmless expression like 1<c>1, and sort the answers by WHICH message comes back
chain.why: this app has two rejection messages and they mean opposite things. One is the filter; the other is PHP's own ParseError, which means the character reached the evaluator and only the surrounding syntax was wrong. Reading them as one 'blocked' bucket hides the entire attack surface: 30 characters that look rejected are in fact accepted

chain.action: measure the LENGTH limit separately, with a valid expression of growing size
chain.why: the same message is returned for an over-long payload as for a forbidden character, so a working technique reads as a filtered one the moment the payload grows. Here the cap is strlen >= 100, and the first correct payload built was 170 bytes and looked like a filter hit

chain.action: find a string SOURCE that needs no quotes. PHP prints the degenerate floats as text, so (1/0) is INF, (0/0) is NAN and (1/3)/(10**20) is scientific notation, and a string offset cuts single characters out of them
chain.why: with both quotes filtered there is no literal at all, and this is the generic way back in: any expression whose string cast contains letters is a literal. It is enough on its own -- the GF(2) span of the bytes those yield covers all of ASCII -- but it costs roughly forty characters per target byte

chain.action: test a bare underscore on its own. It returned the string _, which says the runtime is PHP 7 and an undefined constant still degrades to its own name
chain.why: that single-character probe is the whole solve. PHP identifiers accept the bytes 0x80-0xFF, and a character filter written as [a-z'"] does not touch them, so any run of high bytes is a free string literal costing ONE byte per character

chain.action: complement the target with ~: send the constant made of the bitwise complements of the wanted ASCII, and wrap it in ~(...). Use shell_exec, not system: (~(<~shell_exec>))(~(<~command>)) is a complete call in 20 bytes plus the command
chain.why: ~ on a string is bytewise, so ~ of a 0x80-0xFF run is the ASCII you wanted. It reduces a forty-bytes-per-character XOR chain to one byte per character, which is what brings the payload inside the 99-byte cap. The command string is built the same way, so it may contain quotes, pipes and spaces freely -- the filter never sees them. shell_exec costs four more bytes than system and is worth every one of them: system RETURNS only the last line and it is the return value the page prints, so `ls /` renders www, while shell_exec renders the whole listing

first_confirming_probe.expected: the page renders _ . An undefined constant became its own name, so the runtime is PHP 7.x and the high-byte constant trick is available
first_confirming_probe.falsifier: it renders an error or nothing. On PHP 8 an undefined constant is an Error, so this route is closed and the chain falls back to the slower INF/NAN plus XOR construction in step 3

blast_radius: This ends in command execution as the web user, so treat every command as a write. Keep them read-only (id, ls, cat) and never redirect output into the document root on a shared instance. Nothing was written to the target in this solve. The 99-byte cap is an accidental safety rail: it is too small for most destructive one-liners, which is a reason not to work around it by dropping a file.

verification.evidence: Live HTB instance. The character sweep returned the filter message for exactly the 54 characters [a-zA-Z"'] and nothing else. GET /?formula=_ rendered _ . GET /?formula=~(%8C%86%8C%8B%9A%92) rendered system. GET /?formula=(~(%8C%86%8C%8B%9A%92))(~(%96%9B)) rendered uid=1000(www) gid=1000(www) groups=1000(www). ls / showed a randomised flagYrsQz at the root and cat of it returned the flag. Recorded in challenges/pcalc/state.json through tools/hooks.py post-probe (confirms, evidence-kind impact) and pre-flag (source live-response). Afterwards the application source was read through the same primitive and confirms every inference: models/CalcModel.php rejects on strlen($formula) >= 100 || preg_match_all('/[a-z\'"]+/i', $formula), then runs eval('$pcalc = ' . $formula . ';') and catches ParseError; php -v reports PHP 7.4.33. Independently reproduced in the same session by a separate agent that reached the same flag by a different route -- shell_exec rather than system -- and binary-searched the same cap to 99 OK / 100 blocked before the source was read.

reuse_when: a filter is written as a character DENYLIST in front of an evaluator: enumerate the whole printable set one character at a time rather than guessing, and separate the filter's message from the evaluator's error message. Those two answers are the map

both quote characters are filtered and a string is still needed: look for expressions whose string cast contains letters. In PHP that is INF, -INF, NAN and scientific notation; in other runtimes it is the spelling of true/false/null, an exception message, or a type name

any PHP 7 target where letters are filtered: try a bare _ first. An undefined constant degrading to its own name turns every identifier-legal byte into a free string literal, and identifiers accept 0x80-0xFF
a payload that is correct but too long: reach for ~ on a high-byte run before optimising an XOR chain. One byte per character instead of forty is usually the difference between over and under a cap

a command string that must contain characters the filter blocks: build the STRING with the bypass and the filter never sees its contents, so quotes, pipes, spaces and redirections all become available again
known_traps: the two rejection messages mean opposite things and look equally final. 'dont bite the hand that feeds you human' is the filter; 'report to the nearest galactic federation agency' is a caught ParseError, which means the character got through. Thirty characters that appear blocked in a naive sweep are actually accepted.

the filter message is ALSO returned for an over-long payload, because the length check and the character check share one branch. A correct technique therefore reads as a filtered one as soon as the payload grows; measure the cap on its own before concluding a character is forbidden. The first working construction here was 170 bytes and was misread as a filter hit.
a falsy result renders no alert at all, so an empty page is 0, false or the empty string, not a failure. Do not treat a blank answer as a dead probe.

eval is an ASSIGNMENT here, eval('$pcalc = ' . $formula . ';'), not a return. Anything after a ; is evaluated but discarded, which is why 1;2 answers 1 -- useful to know before building a multi-statement payload that appears to be ignored.

(0/0)[1] answers nothing: a float cannot be offset. Concatenate first, and concatenate with a PARENTHESISED digit -- (0/0).1 is a parse error because .1 lexes as the float 0.1, while (0/0).(1) is the string NAN1.

system() prints its output directly and RETURNS only the last line, and it is the return value that lands in the template, so ls / renders just www and looks like a broken payload. Measured on this target: system -> 'www', shell_exec -> the full 22-entry listing. Use shell_exec, or pipe through tr.
the high-byte constant route is PHP 7 only. PHP 8.0 turns an undefined constant into an Error, so the same payload dies there and the fallback is the much longer INF/NAN plus XOR construction.
